blocks.path: Heart attack
s: A heart attack happens when blood flow to your heart is blocked.
It can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: Symptoms of a heart attack may include:

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: chest pain which may feel like crushing or squeezing on your chest – the pain may also spread to your arm, neck and jaw

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: feeling short of breath

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting)

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: feeling like you have indigestion – you may have a burning feeling in your chest and feel full or bloated

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: sweating

blocks.path: Heart attack > Symptoms of a heart attack
s: pale, blue or grey skin – on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: you have chest pain that feels tight or like squeezing on your chest

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: you have chest pain that's spreading to your arms, neck or jaw

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: you're having severe difficulty breathing – you're gasping, choking or not able to get words out

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: your lips or skin are pale, blue or grey – on brown or black skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: someone has passed out and is not responding normally

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: Do not drive yourself to A&E.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
s: you're suddenly more short of breath than usual

blocks.path: Heart attack > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
s: you have chest pain and you feel sick or are being sick

blocks.path: Heart attack > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
s: you have chest pain and you feel like your heart is racing, going too slowly, skipping a beat or have a fluttering feeling in your chest

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: If you think you or someone else is having a heart attack, there are some things you can do while you wait for help.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: Sit and rest on the floor in a comfortable position, with your knees bent and your back supported.
If you cannot do this, you can also sit on a chair.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: Take aspirin (300mg) if you have any – do not give aspirin to someone who has an aspirin allergy.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: If you have angina, take your glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray if you have it with you.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: Keep checking someone who may be having a heart attack to make sure they're still responding and breathing.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: If someone stops responding to you and stops breathing, start CPR.

blocks.path: Heart attack > While you're waiting for medical help
s: Find out how to do CPR on the St John Ambulance website.

blocks.path: Heart attack > How a heart attack is diagnosed
s: You'll need tests including an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests to find out if you're having a heart attack.

blocks.path: Heart attack > How a heart attack is diagnosed
s: If these tests show you're having a heart attack, you may have further tests such as:

blocks.path: Heart attack > How a heart attack is diagnosed
s: an echocardiogram, which can find out if your heart has been damaged

blocks.path: Heart attack > How a heart attack is diagnosed
s: a coronary angiogram, which can find out exactly where the blood flow to your heart is blocked – the blockage may be treated at the same time

blocks.path: Heart attack > How a heart attack is diagnosed
s: A doctor will discuss what your test results may mean for you.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: You'll need treatment in hospital for a heart attack.
Your treatment will depend on how severe it is.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: Treatments may include:

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: medicines to treat the blockage in your arteries and improve blood flow to your heart

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: a procedure to improve blood flow to your heart (coronary angioplasty) – this involves opening blocked arteries using a small plastic tube called a stent

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: surgery where arteries are taken from another part of your body and used in your heart to take blood around a blocked artery (coronary artery bypass)

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: A heart attack is a life-threatening condition and cannot always be treated.
There's a chance someone who has one may die.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: Medicines after a heart attack

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: You will be given medicines to take long-term after having a heart attack.
They treat the causes of your heart attack and help reduce your risk of having another one.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: These medicines may include:

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: antiplatelets to help stop your arteries getting blocked

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: statins to lower your cholesterol

blocks.path: Heart attack > Treatments for a heart attack
s: other medicines to lower high blood pressure, such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: Heart attacks affect people in different ways.
For some, it may take several weeks to recover, but there will be little impact on their life.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: For others, recovery can take months or years.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: After having a heart attack, you'll usually:

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: need to rest, including taking time off work

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: be referred to cardiac rehabilitation to help with your recovery – this may involve attending appointments in-person, or taking part remotely from home using video calls or apps

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: Most people can continue with their normal activities once they've recovered.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Recovering from a heart attack
s: You may feel anxious or worried about getting back to your usual tasks or going back to work.
Talk to your GP if you're feeling anxious or you have low mood after having a heart attack.
They can help you get support.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: Heart attacks are usually caused by a blood clot stopping enough blood getting to your heart.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: You're more likely to have a heart attack if you:

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: smoke

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: have high blood pressure

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: have high cholesterol

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: have a close relative who's had a heart attack

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: have diabetes

blocks.path: Heart attack > Causes of a heart attack
s: are living with overweight or obesity

blocks.path: Heart attack > Reducing your risk of having a heart attack
s: You cannot always prevent a heart attack, but there are lifestyle changes you can make to reduce your risk of having one.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Reducing your risk of having a heart attack > Do stop smoking try to keep your cholesterol at a healthy level try to keep your blood pressure at a healthy level eat a healthy, balanced diet reduce the amount of salt and saturated fat you eat try to maintain a healthy weight exercise regularly cut down on alcohol Support after a heart attack You may find it helpful to get emotional support from other people who've had a heart attack, either at a local group or online. There are also national charities that can offer more information and support. British Heart Foundation
s: Information and support for anyone affected by heart conditions, including local and online support services.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Heart attack is different to cardiac arrest
s: Cardiac arrest is when your heart stops suddenly and causes you to lose consciousness.
It's life-threatening but different to a heart attack, and needs different treatment.

blocks.path: Heart attack > Heart attack is different to cardiac arrest
s: The British Heart Foundation website has more information about cardiac arrest.
